body.p: Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47 and 135-145 were previously pending in this application.1 By this amendment, claim 1 has been amended and is supported by the specification as originally filed, for example, on and page 7, lines 16-26 and page 19, lines 16-22. New claims 147 and 148 have been added and are supported by the specification as originally filed, for example. on page 20, lines 22-33.
No new matter has been added. Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, 135-145, 147, and 148 are currently pending in this application for examination, with claim 1 being independent.

The undersigned thanks Examiner Thompson for the courtesy of a telephone interview conducted on January 5, 2022. During the interview, the rejection of independent claim 1 and associated dependent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 103 in view of Rylander, et al., U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2013/0338627 ("Rylander"), Szunerits, et al., "Sensing using Localised Surface Plasmon Resonance Sensors," Chem. Comm., 2012, 48, 8999-9010 ("Szunerits"), Hosokawa, et al., Nanoparticle Technology Handbook, 2007, pg. 365 ("Hosokawa"), and Jardemark, et al., U.S. Pat. Apl. Pub. No. 2004/0182707 ("Jardemark") or Ginaven, et al., U.S. Pat. No. 5,457,041 ("Ginaven") were discussed. The undersigned noted that it would not have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to modify Rylander by attaching particles to the needle taught in Rylander, given that the goal of Rylander is the insertion of the needle through the skin, which would have "scraped" off any particles present, thereby negating any potential functionality of the particles and any motivation to make such a modification to Rylander. Examiner Thompson suggested emphasizing this difference with Rylander, amending the claims to better claim how the device operates, and reviewing MPEP § 2114 and § 2111.04 (generally discussing intended use). Further remarks responsive to each of these are now presented.

body.h1: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. # 103 in view of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or
body.p: Claims 1-3, 5, 30, 37, 42, 47, and 135-141 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Szunerits, and in further view of Hosokawa, and in even further view of Jardemark or Ginaven.
Independent claim 1 has been amended to recite that the member is configured to guide

and/or direct light to analyze the cell and the at least one particle is configured to facilitate analysis of the cell. Rylander fails to teach or suggest these features. Instead, Rylander discloses systems for delivering exogenous photoabsorbers such as nanoparticles to tissue regions for targeted treatment (e.g., cancer treatment) of the tissue. See, for example, paragraph [0295] of Rylander, which states that an application of laser energy delivered via the needles to the target tissue containing nanomaterials induces selective photothermal or photochemical damage to the target tissue. Accordingly, the nanoparticles described in Rylander are configured for cancer therapy, not for analysis of a cell, as recited in amended independent claim 1.

Furthermore, Rylander nowhere teaches or suggests a particle attached to the end portion via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member, wherein the adhesive comprises at least one of a polymer or an epoxy, as claim 1 recites. The Patent Office alleges that paragraphs [0303] and [0320] of Rylander are "interpreted as teaching an article that is capable of having a particle immobilized relative to the end portion of the member via an adhesive material positioned between the particle and the end portion of the member." See page 7 of the Office Action. Rylander, however, does not teach or suggest any adhesive for adhering particles, let alone an adhesive positioned between the particle and the end portion of the member, as recited in independent claim 1. In fact, Rylander teaches the opposite: that nanoparticles are not adhered, but instead are to be delivered into specific tissue regions for targeted treatment. The nanoparticles may be delivered through a hollow fiber. See paragraph [0295]. Adding an adhesive would therefore prevent the Rylander device from achieving its intended purpose. Accordingly, Rylander teaches away from such a modification.
Paragraph [0303], cited by the Patent Office, similarly teaches that a hollow core fiber
(HCF) may be affixed within the bore of a needle and attached to a solution of single-walled carbon

nanohorns (SWNHs) via plastic tubing. The HCF is then used to deliver the SWNHs . See paragraphs [0303] of Rylander. Paragraph [0320] appears to teach that such hollow core fibers can also be used for fat removal or fat infusion, but does not appear to be related to particles, let alone immobilized particles. Thus, neither paragraphs [0303] nor [0320] teach or suggest immobilized particles, let alone the use of an adhesive to immobilize such particles.

Regarding MPEP § 2114, § 2111.04 and intended use, it is submitted that the recitations in claim 1 of at least one particle, and an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member, are positively recited structural limitations, rather than an intended use for the device. See the Office Action, page 9. "[A]pparatus claims cover what a device is, not what a device does." MPEP § 2114(II) (citing Hewlett-Packard Co.v.Bausch & Lomb Inc., 909 F.2d 1464, 1469, 15 USPQ2d 1525, 1528 (Fed. Cir. 1990), emphasis in original). In this case, claim 1 recites "An article... comprising... at least one particle attached to the end portion of the member... wherein the at least one particle is attached to the end portion of the member via an adhesive...." These features are present in the claimed device, regardless of what the device does or is used for, or how the device was made. Accordingly, the at least one particle and the adhesive recited in independent claim 1 should not be treated as an intended use of the device.
With respect to the remaining references, it is not seen how Szunerits, Hosokawa, and

Jardemark or Ginaven cure the deficiencies of Rylander in order to reach the pending claims. For instance, nowhere do any of Szunerits, Hosokawa, Jardemark, or Ginaven teach or suggest: (i) a member comprising a starting portion having a substantially constant average cross-sectional diameter of at least about 100 micrometers; (ii) the member comprising an end portion for insertion into a cell having a substantially constant average cross-sectional diameter of less than 100 nm; (iii) at least one particle attached to the end portion via an adhesive positioned between the at least one particle and the end portion of the member, wherein the adhesive comprises at least one of a polymer or an epoxy; or (iv) the member being configured to guide and/or direct light to analyze the cell and the at least one particle being configured to facilitate analysis of the cell, as recited in amended independent claim 1. Both Szunerits and Hosokawa, for example, are generally directed to detection techniques using metal particles, but neither reference teaches nor suggests that particles may be used for the analysis of a cell. Furthermore, Jardemark is generally directed to

measuring the electrical properties of a cell using a nanoelectrode, and Ginaven is generally directed to the delivery of biological substances (e.g., DNA) to a cell to facilitate, for example, gene implantation.

For at least the reasons outlined above, the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or Ginaven does not render amended independent claim 1 obvious, and claim 1 is believed to be patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or Ginaven. The remaining claims that stand rejected on these grounds depend from independent claim 1, and are therefore also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or Ginaven for at least these reasons. Withdrawal of the claim rejections is therefore respectfully requested.
body.h1: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. # 103 in view of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, Jardemark or Ginaven,
body.p: Dependent claims 142, 143, and 145 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being

unpatentable over Rylander in view of Szunerits, and in further view of Hosokawa, and in even further view of Jardemark or Ginaven, and in even further view of Goncalves, et al., "Self- Assembled Hydrogel Nanoparticles for Drug Delivery Applications," Materials, 2010, 3, 1420- 1460 ("Goncalves").
Claims 142, 143, and 145 depend from independent claim 1, which is patentable over

Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or Ginaven for at least the reasons outlined above. Goncalves fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or Ginaven noted above with respect to independent claim 1. Accordingly, claims 142, 143, and 145 are also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, Jardemark or Ginaven, and Goncalves. In addition, it is not conceded that Goncalves teaches any of the features recited in claims 142, 143, and 145, and it is not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, Jardemark or Ginaven, and Goncalves in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejections on this ground is respectfully requested.

body.p: Dependent claim 144 stands rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Rylander in view of Szunerits, and in further view of Hosokawa, and in even further in view of Jardemark or Ginaven, and in even further view of Gautam, et al., "Adsorption kinetics of ammonia sensing by graphene films decorated with platinum nanoparticles," Journal of Applied Physics, 2012, 111, 094317 ("Gautam").

Claim 144 depends from independent claim 1, which is patentable over Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or Ginaven for at least the reasons outlined above. Gautam fails to cure the deficiencies of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, and Jardemark or Ginaven noted above with respect to independent claim 1. Accordingly, claim 144 is also patentable over the combination of Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, Jardemark or Ginaven, and Gautam. In addition, it is not conceded that Gautam teaches any of the features recited in claim 144, and it is not conceded that it would have been obvious to combine Rylander, Szunerits, Hosokawa, Jardemark or Ginaven, and Gautam in the manner suggested in the Office Action. Withdrawal of the claim rejection on this ground is respectfully requested.
